title: How Invasive Rats Mess with Coral Reef Food Webs
gist: A short teaser on a study in Ecology by Lancaster University and University of Texas biologists quantifying how introduced black rats on Indian Ocean islands propagate through seabird populations into adjacent coral reef food webs. The dek promises the effect is "not always a bad thing" but the visible text stops before delivering that nuance, covering only the negative terrestrial-to-marine cascade.

insights.claim: The ecological impact of introduced rats on islands extends past terrestrial habitats into adjacent coral reefs, meaning a land-based invasive species is a measurable driver of marine ecosystem state.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: Reef health assessments and blue-carbon or conservation-credit models that ignore island pest status are missing a first-order variable.
insights.quote: ecological impacts of rats on islands extend far beyond their terrestrial habitats
insights.locator: Now, a recent study in the journal Ecology

insights.claim: Seabird densities are roughly 760 times greater on rat-free islands than on rat-infested ones, and the resulting influx of guano nutrients fertilizes surrounding reefs so corals grow faster and support more fish.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: A 760x differential is an unusually large natural-experiment effect size — rat eradication is one of the highest-leverage interventions available per dollar in reef conservation.
insights.quote: densities of seabirds to be about 760 times greater on rat-free islands, resulting in an influx of nutrients from bird droppings that “fertilize” the surrounding reefs
insights.locator: A previous study showed densities of seabirds

insights.claim: Island biodiversity only begins to rebound once rats are removed, as demonstrated at Lord Howe Island in Australia and Redonda in the Caribbean.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: Eradication has documented reference cases, which makes it fundable and measurable — a template for conservation programs seeking verifiable outcomes.
insights.locator: It’s only when rats are removed from islands

insights.claim: The Indian Ocean study islands were chosen because black rats were introduced several hundred years ago while the islands otherwise have no direct human impacts, isolating the rat variable from confounding development effects.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: A clean natural experiment makes this causal claim more transferable than typical correlational reef studies.
